1.1.i: Standard form is a way of writing very big or very small numbers so you can see their size at a glance: the power of 10 tells you the size, the number in front tells you the detail.
1.1.h: Because 10^p × 10^q = 10^(p+q), products of standard-form numbers split into a product of the fronts and a sum of the powers. If the new front falls outside 1 ≤ a < 10, you shift one factor of 10 between the front and the power.
1.1.q: Calculate (3 × 10⁵) × (6 × 10⁻²) and give the answer in standard form.
s: Multiply the fronts: 3 × 6 = 18.
Multiplication can be done in any order, so the fronts and the powers can be dealt with separately.
Add the powers: 10⁵ × 10⁻² = 10³.
Multiplying powers of the same base adds the exponents.
18 is not between 1 and 10, so it isn't standard form yet; moving one factor of 10 into the power fixes that.

Standard form: a is the number in front, k is the whole-number power of 10.
When a question asks for the form a × 10^k. Always check 1 ≤ a < 10, and never leave a calculator's E notation.

1.2.i: An arithmetic sequence is a staircase with equal steps. Knowing the first step and the step size tells you every other step without listing them.
1.2.h: The nth term is linear in n, with gradient d. The sum formula comes from writing the series forwards and backwards and adding: every pair adds to u₁ + uₙ and there are n pairs, so 2Sₙ = n(u₁ + uₙ).
1.2.q: A sequence has u₁ = 7 and d = 4. Find u₂₀ and S₂₀.
s: To get from term 1 to term 20 you take 19 steps, not 20, which is why the formula has n − 1.
Now the first and last terms are known, so the shorter form of the sum is the quickest and least error-prone.

nth term: u₁ first term, d common difference, n position of the term.
When terms change by a constant amount and you need one term or its position. n must be a positive integer.
Sum of n terms: n number of terms, u₁ first term, d common difference, uₙ last term.
When adding the first n terms of an arithmetic sequence. Use the (u₁ + uₙ) form if the last term is known.

1.3.i: A geometric sequence multiplies by the same number every time, so it grows or shrinks faster and faster, like money earning interest on its interest.
1.3.h: The nth term is an exponential function of n. Multiply Sₙ by r and subtract from Sₙ: all the middle terms cancel, leaving Sₙ(r − 1) = u₁(rⁿ − 1), which is where the sum formula comes from.
1.3.q: A sequence starts 5, 10, 20, … Find u₈ and S₈.
s: The ratio between consecutive terms is what defines the sequence; checking 20 ÷ 10 = 2 confirms it is geometric.
From term 1 to term 8 there are 7 multiplications by r.
Use the form with r − 1 on the bottom when r > 1, so that top and bottom are both positive.

nth term: u₁ first term, r common ratio, n position of the term.
When each term is a fixed multiple of the one before. n is a positive integer.
Sum of n terms: u₁ first term, r common ratio, n number of terms.
When adding n terms of a geometric sequence. Not valid for r = 1 (then the sum is n × u₁).

1.4.i: Compound interest means this year's interest also earns interest. Every period the money is multiplied by the same factor, so it is a geometric sequence in disguise.
1.4.h: Splitting the year into k periods divides the rate by k but multiplies the number of periods by k. To find a real value after inflation, reduce the interest rate by the inflation rate, or divide the future value by the inflation growth factor.
1.4.q: €2000 is invested at 3% per year compounded monthly. Find its value after 5 years.
s: Identify PV = 2000, r = 3, k = 12, n = 5.
Naming each value first prevents mixing up periods per year with number of years.
Each month earns 3/12 % and there are 60 months in 5 years.
Keep full accuracy on the calculator; money answers are given to 2 decimal places or as the question asks.

Compound interest: PV present value, r% nominal yearly rate, k compounding periods per year, n years, FV future value.
When interest is added to the balance k times a year. For annual compounding k = 1.
Depreciation: PV starting value, r% loss per year, n years, FV value after n years.
When something loses a fixed percentage of its current value each period.

1.5.i: A logarithm is a question: what power do I need? Logs undo exponentials the same way subtraction undoes addition.
1.5.h: Because exponentials and logs are inverse functions, taking a log brings an unknown power down to where you can solve for it. ln is simply log with base e, the base that appears naturally in continuous growth.
s: Divide by 3: 2ˣ = 16.
The power must be alone before a log can undo it.
Write x = log₂ 16.
This is the definition of a logarithm: x is the power of 2 that gives 16.
x = 4, because 2⁴ = 16.
Substituting back into the power is a quick check that the log was read correctly.

Exponent laws: a is the base; m and n are the exponents.
When the bases are the same. They do not apply to sums like aᵐ + aⁿ.
Definition of a logarithm: a is the base, x the power, b the result.
To switch between power form and log form. Needs a > 0, a ≠ 1 and b > 0.

1.6.i: A rounded number really stands for a small range of possible values. Bounds give that range, and percentage error says how far off an estimate is compared with the true size.
1.6.h: When combining bounded values, choose the bound that pushes the result the way you want: the largest quotient comes from the largest numerator over the smallest denominator. Error is relative to the exact value, which is why it goes on the bottom.
1.6.q: A length is measured as 12 cm, to the nearest cm. The exact length is 12.4 cm. Find the bounds of the measurement and the percentage error.
s: Lower bound 11.5, upper bound 12.5.
Nearest cm means half a unit either side of the rounded value.
The approximate value goes first and the exact value goes on the bottom, because error is measured against the truth.
Percentage error is reported as a positive size; the modulus removes the sign.

Percentage error: v_A approximate value, v_E exact value.
When comparing an estimate or rounded value with the exact one. Always divide by the exact value.

1.7.i: A loan is a race between interest pushing the debt up and your payments pushing it down. Early on most of each payment is interest; near the end most of it reduces the debt.
1.7.h: An amortization is a geometric series: each payment's present value is discounted by one more period. The finance app solves that series for you, and the sign of each amount says which way the money moves from your point of view.
1.7.q: A €10 000 loan is repaid with 48 equal monthly payments of €240. Find the total interest paid.
s: Interest is whatever you pay beyond what you borrowed, so you first need the total of all the payments.
Subtracting the amount borrowed leaves only the cost of borrowing.

Total paid on a loan: PMT payment each period, N number of payments.
Once the payment is known, to find everything paid back over the whole loan.
Interest paid: PMT payment each period, N number of payments, PV amount borrowed.
For the total cost of a loan. Use the size of PMT, ignoring the calculator's negative sign.

1.8.i: Each equation is a condition. A system asks for the numbers that satisfy all the conditions at once, and the calculator does the solving once you have written the conditions down.
1.8.h: n independent linear equations in n unknowns have exactly one solution; dependent ones have none or infinitely many. A polynomial of degree n has at most n real roots, so count them on the graph to be sure you have them all.
1.8.q: Adult tickets cost €8 and child tickets €5. 40 tickets were sold for €263. How many of each?
s: Let a be adults, c children: a + c = 40 and 8a + 5c = 263.
Most of the marks are here: one equation counts tickets, the other counts money.
Solve the system with technology: a = 21, c = 19.
Once the equations are right, the solving is routine.
Substituting into the original words catches errors in forming the equations.

1.9.i: Logs turn multiplying into adding and powers into multiplying, because logs are exponents and exponents already follow those rules.
1.9.h: Each law is an exponent law read backwards. Change of base works because writing x = log_b a as bˣ = a and taking log base c of both sides gives x log_c b = log_c a.
1.9.q: Solve log₂ x + log₂ (x − 2) = 3, for x > 2.
s: Combine: log₂ (x(x − 2)) = 3.
One single log is needed before the log can be removed.
Convert: x(x − 2) = 2³ = 8, so x² − 2x − 8 = 0.
Log form becomes power form by the definition of a logarithm.
x = 4 or x = −2; reject −2.
Logs only exist for positive inputs, so every answer must be tested against the original domain.

Laws of logarithms: a is the base; x and y are the positive numbers being logged; m any real power.
To combine or split logs with the same base. There is no law for log(x + y).
Change of base: a the number, b the old base, c any new base (usually e or 10).
When the base is not the one you want or you need a value from ln or log₁₀.

1.10.i: A fractional power is a root and a power together: the bottom says which root, the top says which power.
1.10.h: The notation has to fit the exponent laws: (x^(1/n))ⁿ = x^(n/n) = x, so x^(1/n) can only be the nth root. Taking the root first usually keeps the numbers small.
s: Taking the root first keeps the numbers small.
Same base being multiplied, so add the exponents: 2/4 + 3/4 = 5/4.

Rational exponents: a positive base, m the power, n the root.
To switch between root and power form. Assume a > 0 so the root is defined.

1.11.i: If each term is a fixed fraction of the last, you keep adding less and less. The total creeps towards a limit it never passes, like walking half the remaining distance each step.
1.11.h: In Sₙ = u₁(1 − rⁿ)/(1 − r), the term rⁿ tends to 0 only when |r| < 1, which leaves u₁/(1 − r). If |r| ≥ 1 the terms do not shrink and no finite total exists.
1.11.q: Find the sum to infinity of 20 + 15 + 11.25 + …
s: You need r both for the formula and to test convergence.
|0.75| < 1, so the sum exists.
The formula means nothing unless this condition holds, and questions often ask you to state it.
Substitute the first term and the ratio.

Sum to infinity: u₁ first term, r common ratio.
Only for a geometric series with |r| < 1.

1.12.i: Complex numbers add a second direction to the number line. A complex number is a point with a real position across and an imaginary position up.
1.12.h: i is defined by i² = −1, and otherwise you use ordinary algebra. Multiplying by the conjugate works because (a + bi)(a − bi) = a² + b², which is real, so it clears i from a denominator.
1.12.q: Write (3 + 2i) ÷ (1 − i) in the form a + bi.
s: Multiply top and bottom by 1 + i.
1 + i is the conjugate of the denominator, the one factor that makes it real.
Expand as usual, then replace i² with −1.
This is a² + b² with a = 1, b = 1.
The required form needs the real and imaginary parts written separately.

Cartesian form: a real part, b imaginary part, i the imaginary unit.
For adding and subtracting, and whenever a + bi is requested.
Conjugate: z* is z with the sign of the imaginary part changed.
To divide complex numbers or to find |z|².

1.13.i: Polar form describes a complex number like a compass direction: how far from the origin and at what angle. That makes multiplying easy, because lengths multiply and angles add.
1.13.h: Euler's form re^(iθ) explains the rules: multiplying adds exponents, so angles add. In AC circuits, sine waves of the same frequency can be added as complex numbers, because their sum is another wave of that frequency.
1.13.q: Let z = 1 + i. Write z in the form re^(iθ) and find z⁸.
s: The modulus is the distance from the origin, by Pythagoras.
θ = arctan(1/1) = π/4.
z is in the first quadrant, so the calculator's arctan is already the right angle.
A power raises the modulus and multiplies the argument.
An angle of 2π is a full turn back to the positive real axis.

Modulus and argument: a real part, b imaginary part, r modulus, θ argument.
To convert a + bi into polar form. Sketch the point first: arctan alone can give the wrong quadrant.
Polar and Euler forms: r modulus, θ argument (radians unless told otherwise).
For products, quotients and powers, or when a question asks for this form.
Products and powers: r₁, r₂ moduli, θ₁, θ₂ arguments, n the power.
When multiplying or raising to a power; for a quotient, divide moduli and subtract arguments.

1.14.i: A matrix is a table of numbers that you can treat as one object. Multiplying matrices combines rows with columns, and an inverse undoes a matrix the way dividing undoes multiplying.
1.14.h: A⁻¹ exists exactly when det A ≠ 0, because a zero determinant means the matrix flattens space and information is lost. Since AB ≠ BA in general, you must multiply by the inverse on the correct side: AX = B gives X = A⁻¹B.
1.14.q: Solve 2x + y = 7 and x − 3y = 0 using a matrix equation.
s: This turns two equations into one equation AX = B.
A non-zero determinant confirms that the inverse exists and the solution is unique.
Multiplying on the left by A⁻¹ cancels A; the order cannot be swapped.
Substituting back is quick and catches sign errors in the inverse.

2 × 2 determinant: a, b are the top row, c, d the bottom row of A.
To test for an inverse, and to find area scale factors.
2 × 2 inverse: a, b, c, d are the entries of A.
Only when ad − bc ≠ 0. For larger matrices use technology.

1.15.i: Most vectors change direction when a matrix acts on them. Eigenvectors are the special ones that only get stretched, and the eigenvalue is the stretch factor.
1.15.h: Writing A = PDP⁻¹ means: change into eigenvector coordinates, stretch, change back. In Aⁿ all the inner P⁻¹P pairs cancel, leaving PDⁿP⁻¹, and powers of a diagonal matrix are just powers of its entries.
s: An eigenvector is non-zero, so A − λI must have no inverse, meaning its determinant is 0.
Expand: λ² − 7λ + 10 = 0.
A 2 × 2 matrix always gives a quadratic in λ.
Check: the eigenvalues must add to the diagonal sum 4 + 3 = 7, and they do.

Characteristic equation: A the matrix, λ an eigenvalue, I the identity matrix.
The first step for finding eigenvalues.
Eigenvector: v a non-zero eigenvector, λ its eigenvalue.
After finding λ: solve (A − λI)v = 0 for the direction of v.
Diagonalization: P has eigenvectors as columns, D has the matching eigenvalues on its diagonal.
For powers of a matrix and long-term behaviour. Keep the order of the eigenvalues in D the same as the columns of P.
